title: The Bill of Rights, One by One
short: Match each of the first ten amendments to what it protects: the First (religion, speech, press, assembly, petition) to the Tenth (powers reserved to the states or the people).
trouble: Students mix up the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth. Fourth: searches and seizures; Fifth: self-incrimination, double jeopardy, due process, takings; Sixth: speedy public jury trial and a lawyer.

blocks.html: You saw how the Bill of Rights came out of the ratification fight and how amendments are made. Madison proposed the amendments in 1789, and ten were ratified in 1791. Civil liberties are the freedoms these amendments protect from government interference. Here they are one by one.

head: Amendment
What it protects
rows: First
religion (no establishment, free exercise), speech, press, assembly, petition
Second
the right to keep and bear arms
Third
no soldiers quartered in homes in peacetime without the owner's consent
Fourth
no unreasonable searches and seizures; warrants need probable cause
Fifth
grand jury for serious federal crimes; no double jeopardy; no forced self-incrimination; due process; just compensation for property taken
Sixth
a speedy, public trial by an impartial jury; to know the charges; to confront and call witnesses; a lawyer
Seventh
a jury in federal civil suits over twenty dollars
Eighth
no excessive bail or fines; no cruel and unusual punishments
Ninth
listing some rights does not deny others kept by the people
Tenth
powers not given to the national government are reserved to the states or the people

blocks.html: Notice the pattern. The First protects belief and expression. The Second and Third grew from colonial complaints about standing armies and troops in homes. The Fourth through Eighth are mostly about the criminal process, from the search to the sentence: what you would want if you were ever accused. The Ninth and Tenth are about what the list does not do: it does not give government every power left unlisted, and it does not take away rights left unlisted.

marks.note: The core protection: not every search, only unreasonable ones.
A warrant needs good reason to believe evidence of a crime will be found.

marks.text: particularly describing the place to be searched
marks.note: No general warrants that let officers search anywhere.

blocks.cap: The Fourth Amendment, with its key phrases.

blocks.html: First: expression and religion. Second: arms. Third: quartering. Fourth: searches. Fifth: self-incrimination, double jeopardy, due process, takings. Sixth: jury trial and a lawyer. Seventh: civil juries. Eighth: bail and punishment. Ninth: other rights. Tenth: reserved powers.

blocks.title: Which amendment?
blocks.q: Police want to look through a suspect's car without a warrant. Which amendment applies?
steps: The question is about a search.
Searches and seizures are the Fourth Amendment.

blocks.title: Fifth or Sixth?
blocks.q: A defendant says, "I won't testify; I don't have to," and also asks for a lawyer. Which amendments?
steps: Refusing to be a witness against yourself: the Fifth ("pleading the Fifth").
The right to the assistance of counsel: the Sixth.

blocks.html: Mixing up the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth. Memory aid in order of a case: Fourth, the search; Fifth, the questioning ("I plead the Fifth") and being tried twice; Sixth, the trial itself, with a jury and a lawyer.
